CANNES, France (CNN) -- After eleven days, hundreds of screenings and thousands of snaps from the paparazzi, there could only be one Palme d'Or winner. Austrian director Michael Haneke hugs the president of the Cannes jury, French actress Isabelle Huppert. "The White Ribbon," by Austrian director Michael Haneke, was awarded the prize for its depiction of the cruel punishments meted out at a rural German school before the First World War. "The Palme d'Or is the best prize a filmmaker can win," said Haneke at a press conference following his award. "I am not proud, but I am very happy. In my opinion, it's silly to be proud." It was a case of fifth time lucky for Haneke, who has previously been nominated for the award for "Funny Games" (1997), "Code Unknown" (2000), "The Piano Teacher" (2001) and "Hidden" (2005). "There are always rumors at the festival, and one must not take them seriously," the director said. "When I presented "Hidden" [in 2005], everyone was telling me I was going to win the Palme. And I didn't get it." Jury president Isabelle Huppert, the French actress who won the best actress prize at the 2001 festival for "The Piano Teacher," said she was delighted to have the chance to honor her former director. "I think I always loved him as a director, and that's why I've worked with him before," she said at the post-awards press conference. "To me, the movie is very philosophical. And his style, and his direction are totally ethical in my mind. That's what I wanted to reward." The American actress Robin Wright Penn, who also sat on the festival jury, laughed off rumors that the decision was hotly disputed. "There have been rumors circulating that we were fighting in the room," she told the press conference. "The beauty about loving each other ... [is that] we could disagree, and we still love each other. I felt like we built a consensus among us," she said. "It was like being on "Big Brother," except you could go to the movies," added British screenwriter and fellow juror Hanif Kureishi. "Some of the films are very long," he joked. Elsewhere, Charlotte Gainsbourg won the best actress prize for her shocking turn in Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," featuring scenes of genital mutilation that left audiences stunned. Christolph Waltz won best actor for his role in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," while Brillante Mendoza secured the best director gong for "Kinatay." The jury prize was shared by Korean auteur Park Chan-Wook's vampire film "Thirst," and Andrea Arnold's "Fish Tank," while the grand prix went to "The Prophet," by director Jacques Audiard.

# Michael Haneke Wins Palme d'Or for "The White Ribbon" at 2009 Cannes Film Festival

Austrian director Michael Haneke claimed the Palme d'Or, the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival, for his film **"The White Ribbon"** (German: *Das weiße Band*) at the 62nd edition of the festival in May 2009.

## About the Winning Film

"The White Ribbon" is a black-and-white drama set in a small Protestant village in northern Germany on the eve of World War I (1913–1914). The film explores strange and disturbing events that occur in the community, examining themes of authoritarianism, repression, and the roots of violence—often interpreted as an allegory for the origins of fascism and the conditions that gave rise to Nazism in the generation depicted.

The jury for the 2009 festival was presided over by French actress **Isabelle Huppert**, who had previously worked with Haneke on films including "The Piano Teacher."

## Other Major Award Winners at the 2009 Festival

- **Grand Prix:** *A Prophet* (*Un prophète*), directed by Jacques Audiard — a French crime drama about a young man's rise within the prison system.

- **Best Director:** Brillante Mendoza for *Kinatay* (Philippines) — a controversial and divisive choice.

- **Best Actress:** Charlotte Gainsbourg for her performance in Lars von Trier's *Antichrist*.

- **Best Actor:** Christoph Waltz for his role as SS officer Hans Landa in Quentin Tarantino's *Inglourious Basterds*.

- **Best Screenplay:** Mei Feng for *Spring Fever* (*Chun feng chen zui de ye wan*), directed by Lou Ye.

- **Jury Prize:** Shared between *Fish Tank* (Andrea Arnold) and *Thirst* (Park Chan-wook).

- **Caméra d'Or** (best first feature): *Samson and Delilah*, directed by Warwick Thornton (Australia).

## Significance

This win marked a career high point for Haneke, cementing his reputation as one of Europe's most acclaimed auteurs. "The White Ribbon" went on to receive further honors, including the **Golden Globe for Best Foreign Language Film** and an **Academy Award nomination** in the same category. Haneke would go on to win a second Palme d'Or just three years later, in 2012, for *Amour*—making him one of the select few directors to win the award twice.

**CANNES, France** — Michael Haneke, the Austrian filmmaker known for his uncompromising and often disquieting cinema, captured the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival for "The White Ribbon," a stark meditation on the roots of violence set in a German village on the eve of the First World War.

The victory marks a significant milestone for Haneke, a perennial presence at the festival who has long been recognized as one of European cinema's most rigorous and provocative voices.

## A Portrait of Encroaching Darkness

Shot in luminous black-and-white, "The White Ribbon" (originally titled "Das weiße Band") unfolds in a fictional Protestant village in northern Germany between 1913 and 1914. The film chronicles a series of mysterious and unsettling incidents—accidents, punishments, and acts of cruelty—that ripple through a community governed by strict patriarchal authority, rigid religious discipline, and repressed emotion.

Through the eyes of a village schoolteacher who narrates the events years later, Haneke constructs a chilling examination of authoritarianism and the psychological conditioning of children. The white ribbon of the title refers to a band tied to the children as a reminder of the purity and innocence they are meant to embody—even as the adult world around them festers with hypocrisy and hidden brutality.

Critics have widely interpreted the film as an allegory exploring the conditions that gave rise to fascism, suggesting how a generation raised under harsh discipline and moral absolutism might later embrace the horrors of the twentieth century.

## A Filmmaker's Long Road to the Top

For Haneke, the Palme d'Or represents the culmination of a distinguished relationship with Cannes. The director had previously competed for the festival's highest honor on multiple occasions, earning acclaim for challenging works including "The Piano Teacher," which won the Grand Prix in 2001, and "Caché" ("Hidden"), which brought him the Best Director prize in 2005.

Known for a cinematic style that is austere, precise, and unflinching in its confrontation of human cruelty, Haneke has built a reputation as a filmmaker who refuses easy answers or comfortable resolutions. "The White Ribbon" was widely regarded by critics as a frontrunner throughout the competition.

The jury, presided over by French actress Isabelle Huppert—herself a longtime Haneke collaborator who delivered a searing performance in his "The Piano Teacher"—faced the delicate task of judging a film by a director with whom several members had personal and professional ties.

Huppert, addressing questions about the selection, emphasized the strength of the film on its own artistic merits, describing it as a work of remarkable power and formal control. Her position as jury president lent particular weight to the decision, given her intimate familiarity with the filmmaker's body of work.

American actress Robin Wright Penn, who served on the jury, joined her colleagues in praising the film's craftsmanship and its haunting examination of how societies transmit fear and control across generations.

British writer Hanif Kureishi, another member of the panel, reflected on the film's thematic ambitions and its unsettling relevance, noting the way Haneke's work interrogates the origins of collective violence and the darker undercurrents beneath ordered, respectable society.

## A Festival of Strong Contenders

Haneke's triumph came in a competitive year that featured notable work from directors around the world. "The White Ribbon" distinguished itself through its formal beauty, its intellectual seriousness, and its refusal to offer the audience any reassuring distance from the disturbing questions it raises.

As Haneke accepted the festival's most coveted prize, his victory affirmed Cannes' longstanding embrace of demanding, artistically ambitious cinema—and cemented his status among the ranks of the world's most essential filmmakers.
